scope.purpose: Claim-bound scientific evidence package for biological phenology

authorized_boundary_requires: an explicit start and end boundary supported by the source
a source locator that permits independent verification

sources.citation: Buentgen U, Bagi I, Fekete O, et al. New Insights into the Complex Relationship between Weight and Maturity of Burgundy Truffles (Tuber aestivum). PLOS ONE. 2017;12:e0170375.
relevant_claims: Observed fruit bodies and maturation classes between June and October in Hungary.
Systematic harvest at the Hungarian site extended from early May to late November, with main peaks from mid-June to mid-August.
Swiss observations included fruit bodies from August through December.
Maturity and fruit-body size were not reliably coupled.
limitations: The principal orchard was outside Italy.
The authors explicitly warn against broad biogeographic generalisation.
Observed harvesting does not provide exact nationwide biological boundaries.

sources.citation: Steidinger BS, et al. The fall of the summer truffle: Recurring hot, dry summers drive fruitbody declines, but not range retractions, in Tuber aestivum. Global Change Biology. 2022.
relevant_claims: Tuber aestivum fruiting overlaps the warm part of the tree growing season.
Recurring hot and dry summers affect fruit-body production.
limitations: The study supports climate sensitivity, not a fixed Italian start/end date.

sources.citation: Salerni E, Perini C, Gardin L. Linking Climate Variables with Tuber borchii Sporocarps Production. Natural Resources. 2014;5:408-418.
relevant_claims: Five natural Italian production areas were assessed.
The highest observed production occurred in February and March.
Production was associated with rainfall and temperature in preceding autumn months.
limitations: A production peak is not a complete inclusive biological window.
The paper does not support classifying every date outside February-March as biologically incompatible.

sources.citation: Iotti M, et al. Development and validation of a real-time PCR assay for detection and quantification of Tuber magnatum in soil. BMC Microbiology. 2012;12:93.
relevant_claims: The paper identifies the Tuber magnatum season as September through December in its Italian study context.
limitations: The label season does not define exact inclusive day boundaries or transition periods.
The primary outcome is soil detection, not national phenological calibration.

sources.citation: Graziosi S, Hall IR, Zambonelli A. The Mysteries of the White Truffle: Its Biology, Ecology and Cultivation. Encyclopedia. 2022;2:1959-1971.
relevant_claims: The review describes the height of the Tuber magnatum season as October through December.
Ecology and life-cycle knowledge remain incomplete.
limitations: A review-level seasonal description is insufficient for exact nationwide day boundaries.

sources.citation: Pacioni G, Leonardi M, Di Carlo P, et al. Instrumental monitoring of the birth and development of truffles in a Tuber melanosporum orchard. Mycorrhiza. 2014;24:65-72.
relevant_claims: The monitored orchard supports a staged developmental model.
Melanin and aroma maturation occurred from approximately mid-October through late December.
Ripe truffles were collected during winter.
limitations: A single orchard model is not an Italy-wide calibration.
The model does not authorize a universal binary in-season/out-of-season boundary.

sources.citation: Paolocci F, Rubini A, Riccioni C, Topini F, Arcioni S. Tuber aestivum and Tuber uncinatum: two morphotypes or two species? FEMS Microbiology Letters. 2004;235:109-115.
relevant_claims: The taxonomic separation of Tuber aestivum and Tuber uncinatum is not supported as a simple independent-species assumption.
limitations: Taxonomic evidence alone does not define phenological boundaries.

sources.citation: Molinier V, van Tuinen D, Chevalier G, et al. A multigene phylogeny demonstrates that Tuber aestivum and Tuber uncinatum are conspecific organisms. Fungal Biology. 2013;117:503-512.
relevant_claims: Tuber aestivum and Tuber uncinatum were resolved as conspecific organisms.
limitations: Commercial morphotypes and local phenology may still differ and require explicit modelling.

sources.citation: Salerni E, Paoli L, Perini C. Combined impact of forest management and climate change on Boletus edulis productivity. Italian Journal of Mycology. 2023;52:76-88.
relevant_claims: Boletus edulis productivity responded to rainfall and temperature extremes and forest treatment.
Weather-event effects were observed with delays on the order of weeks.
limitations: The study does not establish fixed national calendar boundaries.
Productivity response depends on site and management.

sources.citation: Andrew C, Heegaard E, Hoiland K, et al. Explaining European fungal fruiting phenology with climate variability. Ecology. 2018;99:1306-1315.
relevant_claims: Mean fungal fruiting timing changes materially with latitude and altitude.
Climate variability explains substantial variation in fruiting phenology.
limitations: European aggregate evidence cannot supply exact Italy-wide species boundaries.

sources.citation: Kauserud H, Heegaard E, Buentgen U, et al. Warming-induced shift in European mushroom fruiting phenology. PNAS. 2012;109:14488-14493.
relevant_claims: Large dated datasets show that European autumn mushroom fruiting seasons shift and extend with climate.
limitations: No Italian nationwide fixed boundary is provided.

sources.citation: Schenk-Jaeger KM, Egli S, Hanimann D, et al. Introducing Mushroom Fruiting Patterns from the Swiss National Poisons Information Centre. PLOS ONE. 2016;11:e0162314.
relevant_claims: The dated dataset includes Cantharellus cibarius and demonstrates observable, species-specific fruiting patterns.
limitations: Poison-centre contacts are an opportunistic proxy rather than calibrated Italian biological boundaries.
Transferability to Italy is not established.

sources.citation: Buentgen U, Egli S, Galvan JD, et al. Drought-induced changes in the phenology, productivity and diversity of Spanish fungi. Fungal Ecology. 2015;16:6-18.
relevant_claims: Drought altered phenology and productivity of edible fungi including Boletus edulis and Cantharellus cibarius.
limitations: Spanish drought response cannot define exact Italian boundaries.

species_decisions.reason: The May-November interval is directly observed outside Italy and varies with geography and climate; it is not an exact Italy-wide boundary.
Primary taxonomic evidence treats T. uncinatum and T. aestivum as conspecific; a separate calendar must not be fabricated from commercial naming.
February-March is an observed production peak, not a complete inclusive season and not evidence that all other dates are incompatible.
The sources support an autumn to early-winter season, but do not calibrate exact inclusive day boundaries or transitions for all Italy.

supported_observation.approximate_period: mid-October through late December, followed by winter ripeness

species_decisions.reason: The developmental stages are supported at one orchard, but they do not establish a universal Italy-wide binary season.
Fruiting responds to recent weather, altitude, latitude, habitat and management; no fixed national biological window is supported.
Available datasets show climate-sensitive fruiting but do not provide calibrated Italian start/end boundaries.

excluded_inputs.reason: They regulate collection and do not establish biological presence or maturation.
They are not claim-bound scientific evidence.
Useful only for discovery; not accepted as contract authority.

recommended_next_action: Commission or locate claim-bound Italian phenology datasets with explicit observation dates, locations, maturity definitions and coverage for each taxon. Until then, preserve UNKNOWN rather than mapping legal or commercial calendars to biological compatibility.
